items.question: What mistakes do pastors usually make that hurt their ministry?
items.book: The Top Ten Mistakes that Pastors Make
items.text:
Friend, our books name several mistakes that wound a ministry. Pastors choose to bear little fruit, leaving fruitful ground for places where they will gather only a few, when God is glorified by much fruit, as John 15:8 says [1]. Some turn into Pharisees, loving the chief seats and greetings in the markets, as Matthew 23:6-7 describes [2]. Others get their priorities wrong, chasing invitations, honorariums, and the favor of rich and powerful people while neglecting to build their own church and setting aside the young, the children, and the poor [4].

There is also the mistake of downplaying humility, refusing to become like little children who are ready to learn, though Matthew 18:3 says we cannot enter the kingdom unless we become as little children [8]. And some are simply slow about ministry, slow to obey the call of God, not discerning the time [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 3, 7, 8 and 9 of *The Top Ten Mistakes that Pastors Make*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 18:3; Matthew 23:6-7; John 7:6; John 15:8.

items.question: What should I do when one of them is a leader I trained?
items.text:
That is a painful kind of departure, and our books speak to it. When a leader you trained leaves, remember that people eventually do what they see you do, so the one thing that should guide your actions most is that those around you are learning from you [4]. David refused to kill Saul because he would not set a precedent for others to follow [4].

Do not mock or gloat when such a person is in trouble, for "he that is glad at calamities shall not be unpunished" (Proverbs 17:5) [2]. And be open to what God is doing in you through it, for each person who leaves can become a stepping stone to a higher dimension of ministry if you let it [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *Those who leave you*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Kings 11:3-4; Proverbs 17:5; 2 Corinthians 7:11; 1 John 2:18-19.

items.question: How do I start a new church in a town where we have no members?
items.text:
What a good question to bring, and the books speak to it plainly. You do not need a crowd to begin — two or three is enough, for where two or three are gathered in His name, there He is in the midst of them (Matthew 18:20) [6]. One pastor who knew nobody in South Africa started a church there, and the Lighthouse Cathedral began with as few as five people [6]. If you are truly called of God, the only person you need is yourself [6].

Count the cost first, as Luke 14:28 says, sitting down before you build the tower [5]. It will not be easy, and not many want to identify with a small thing [5]. Do not be financially desperate in these early stages; find a job and start as a lay person, so people see you are not ministering for gain [1][2]. And do not be discouraged by small or fluctuating numbers — that is how sheep behave; take no notice of them [3][4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *The Mega Church* and chapter 20 of *Church Planting*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 18:20; Luke 14:28.

items.question: What is true forgiveness?
items.text:
True forgiveness is releasing all hurts, bitterness, and wickedness from your heart, so that you deny the enemy access to your heart [7]. It means dismissing the painful issues, giving up all claims against the one who offended you, cancelling any indebtedness, making no more mention of the matter, stopping resentment and anger, and cancelling any punishment you had planned [7]. As Ephesians 4:32 says, we are to be kind and tenderhearted, forgiving one another even as God for Christ's sake has forgiven us [7].

It also means walking in love and praying for those who offend you, loving your enemies and blessing those who curse you [7]. And a real test of it is being able to pray sincerely for the well-being of the one who hurt you [1].

items.question: People are spreading lies about me in the church. How should I respond?
items.text:
I'm sorry you're carrying this. Our books speak directly to slander, and here is what they say.

Slander from church leaders is especially devastating, because the authority of pastors gives credence to the stories they peddle, and some church leaders are indeed slanderers [1]. Slanderers spread fear through their stories, so that many feel the church is collapsing; but God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love and a sound mind, as 2 Timothy 1:7 says [4]. Your part is to trust the Lord, as Psalm 31:11-14 says: "I trusted in thee, O Lord: I said, Thou art my God" [4].

Remember too that a slanderer reveals secrets, and Scripture says "one who goes about as a slanderer reveals secrets, but one who is trustworthy conceals a matter" (Proverbs 11:13) [7]. People who fall into sin are to be helped up, not pushed further underground, for "Rejoice not against me, O my enemy. When I fall, I shall arise again" [7]. And do not be a destroyer yourself; lay hands on your tongue if necessary, and make sure there is no poison in your tongue [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *Those Who Are Slanderers* and chapter 9 of *Poison: Taming The Tongue*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 31:11-14; Psalms 105:15; Psalms 119:21-24; Proverbs 11:13; 2 Timothy 1:7.

items.question: Why do some Christians who give tithes prosper while others struggle?
items.book: Why Non Tithing Christians Become Poor And Tithing Christians Become Rich
items.text:
Our books speak to this. The tithe is a seed sown in the house of God, and everyone who pays tithes sows a seed and qualifies for a harvest, for "they that sow in tears shall reap in joy" (Psalm 126:5) and "give, and it shall be given unto you; good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over" (Luke 6:38) [3]. Tithing also fulfils the law of humility, which creates wealth, since it makes you bow before your Creator and recognise the God-factor in your existence [5][6].

But the same books say a blessing in one area can be cancelled by a curse from another. Tithing does not work for some because of hidden sins, for "he that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy" (Proverbs 28:13) [1]. Others have wrong desires, and "ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts" (James 4:2-3) [4]. Others are not at peace with the brethren, for "the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace of them that make peace" (James 3:18) [4]. And others have bad marital relationships, so that their prayers are hindered, as 1 Peter 3:7 says [1][4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 14 and 22 of *Why Non Tithing Christians Become Poor And Tithing Christians Become Rich*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 75:6-7; Psalms 126:5; Proverbs 28:13; Matthew 6:33; Luke 6:38; James 3:18; James 4:2-3; 1 Peter 3:7.

items.question: A leader I trained for years has just left the church. How do I handle it?
items.text:
I'm sorry — that is a heavy thing to carry, and I want to walk carefully with you here.

First, guard your own spirit. The event of someone leaving has an effect on your spirit; leavers pollute you with seeds of hurt, anger, hatred, wickedness and revenge, and you will need to pray long and hard to get free from them, or you will fall into bitterness and unforgiveness [4]. David prayed, "Keep me from the jaws of the trap which they have set for me, and from the snares of those who do iniquity" (Psalm 141:9-10) [4].

Be careful how you judge the reasons. Job's friends thought they knew why trouble came on people, and that attitude can open a door for Satan into your own life and ministry [3]. Three pastors once mocked another church's "bad leader" as the reason people left him — and a couple of years later the same thing happened to them, more severely [3]. So examine yourself honestly: the Lord may allow people to leave because you have not continued to follow Him as at the beginning, as Solomon's heart was turned in his old age (1 Kings 11:3-4), or because you have not exerted your authority, since weak leaders cannot establish loyalty and end up with a worse crisis [5]. Yet sometimes, in spite of the most perfect leadership strategies, people still stir up strife against you, and there is nothing you can do about it [4].

On the practical side, the books are direct: if anyone indicates his desire to resign, it is best for him not to stay but to leave immediately, because his heart has already left — "a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump" (1 Corinthians 5:6), and Jesus told Judas, "That thou doest, do quickly" (John 13:27) [7]. A disloyal assistant can do terrible damage if handled wrongly; such people must be restricted, not left free to operate normally, for that is handling them God's way [2].

And do not lose heart. God raised up others when one worship leader turned against him — sometimes the departure of a person heralds the arrival of God's choice for you, as David was revealed when Saul's heart departed from the Lord [6]. If you are open, each person who leaves you will become a stepping stone to a higher dimension of ministry [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 33 of *Victory Secrets*, chapters 1 and 10 of *Those who leave you* and chapter 3 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Kings 11:3-4; Psalms 141:9-10; Proverbs 3:7; John 13:27; 1 Corinthians 5:6; 1 Corinthians 14:33; 2 Corinthians 7:11.

items.question: How do I forgive someone who hurt me very badly?
items.text:
I'm sorry for the hurt you're carrying. Our books speak directly to this.

Forgiveness means releasing all hurts, bitterness and wickedness from your heart, giving up all claims against the person, cancelling any indebtedness, making no more mention of the matter, stopping resentment and anger, and cancelling all punishments you have planned [1]. It is to walk in love and pray for your offender, as Jesus said: love your enemies, bless those who curse you, and pray for those who despitefully use you [1].

One thing that makes it easier is to analyse the offender — as Jesus did on the cross when He prayed, "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do" (Luke 23:34) [2][3]. Your offender may be sick, ignorant or confused, and may not be fully aware of what he is doing [5]. It also helps to analyse your own past sins, considering yourself lest you also be tempted [5]. And remember you are equally in dire need of forgiveness from God, for if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you (Matthew 6:14) [3].

Do not be afraid to forgive — your forgiveness is not the end of the story, for God says, "Vengeance is mine; I will repay" (Romans 12:19-20) [7]. Your duty is to forgive and God's duty is to repay [7]. Forgiveness is a choice that leads to healing; the Lord heals the broken in heart and binds up their wounds (Psalm 147:3), and His Holy Spirit is like oil and balm for your wound [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 18 of *Those Who Are Offended*, chapters 5 and 8 of *Forgiveness Made Easy 3rd Edition* and chapter 59 of *Model Marriage*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 147:3; Matthew 6:14; Luke 23:34; Romans 12:19-20; Ephesians 4:32; Hebrews 12:3.

items.question: A member has stopped coming to church and stopped praying. How do I help them come back to God?
items.text:
Our books speak to this. Staying in fellowship matters: if we walk in the light as He is in the light, we have fellowship one with another (1 John 1:7), and if you are in the light you will go to church and fellowship with other Christians [3]. A Christian who doesn't pray is a Christian who will fall into one temptation after another until he eventually backslides, and an uncommitted Christian is a potential backslider [8]. God expects the believer to be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, planted in the house of the Lord, with somebody to relate to as pastor — you need to belong somewhere [8].

So keep the door open and call them home: it is time to come back home, and staying in fellowship is an important key to receiving the blessings of the Lord [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 9 of *How to Pray* and chapter 7 of *Backsliding*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 119:133; Proverbs 7:10; 1 John 1:7; 1 John 3:22.

items.question: How can a young person stay away from sexual sin?
items.text:
The books speak to this directly, and gently. First, respect your sexuality rather than denying it — a proper respect for youthful lusts, rather than a denial of them, will save you from them [3]. And know that God's will is clear here: "For this is the will of God, your sanctification; that you abstain from sexual immorality" (1 Thessalonians 4:3-4) [2]. So make sexual purity one of your clearest and most energetic goals, and stay away from anyone who would want such a relationship with you [2].

Practically, the books advise no untimely relationships — very young people should not enter into courtship, for "to every thing there is a season" (Ecclesiastes 3:1) — and relationships only unto marriage, since the only intimate relationship God approves of is marriage [5]. Each person must find his own way of keeping himself from fornication; it may be God's will for you to avoid certain books or films, certain friends, or certain places, or to marry young [2]. And do not trifle with this subject: Paul was emphatic that immorality brings the wrath of God (Ephesians 5:5-6) [3].

There is also hope here, not only warning. Holiness is engineered by the Spirit of holiness, not by being older — age has nothing to do with holiness (Romans 1:4) [7]. Young people can live free from sin, because God promises, "I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes" (Ezekiel 36:27) [7]. Many young people have lived relatively sinless and pure lives, keeping the commandments from their youth upwards [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *The Art of Hearing*, chapters 10 and 13 of *Ready@20* and chapter 4 of *Spiritual Dangers*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 3:16; Ecclesiastes 3:1; John 8:46; Romans 1:4; Ephesians 5:5-6; 1 Thessalonians 4:3-4.

items.question: How can my wife and I build a strong marriage?
items.text:
What a good thing to be asking. The books say a happy home does not just happen; it must be developed, and nothing happens by chance [7]. So start with Christ as the foundation and head of your home — when God is the focus of both of you, you draw closer to each other, and that is what makes a happy home [7]. Build your marriage around the church, and let the Word of God be your manual for marriage [2]. Hold regular devotions together, or at least each of you regularly and together when you can, and attend church services together, sitting together [2][3].

Think as a Christian spouse: do nothing out of selfish ambition or vain conceit, but in humility consider others better than yourselves (Philippians 2:3), reconciling the plans you each held before marriage to suit the home, giving up certain interests for its sake, and being ready to compromise rather than always insisting on your own way [3]. Be the best of friends and speak to each other — speaking the truth in love makes you grow up in Christ (Ephesians 4:15) and draws you closer [5]. Speak life, not death, for death and life are in the power of the tongue (Proverbs 18:21) [5]. And have mutual friends as much as possible; if a friendship doesn't sit well with your spouse, it should be discontinued for the stability of the marriage [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 7, 9 and 60 of *Model Marriage*.

Scriptures referenced: Job 32:17-20; Psalms 1:1-6; Proverbs 14:4; Proverbs 18:21; Proverbs 24:3; Luke 6:47-48; Ephesians 4:15; Philippians 2:3; 1 John 4:18.

items.question: There is a woman in our church who manipulates and controls people. How do I deal with her?
items.book: Jezebel, A Woman Out Of Order
items.text:
Our books speak directly to this. A Jezebel must not be allowed to operate freely in the church, and it angers God when she is left unchecked [7]. It takes the collective rebuke of church leadership to deal with a Jezebel; one person identifying her and crying foul is not going to correct or control her [3]. God wants more people to identify the Jezebels in our midst and stop them [3].

Many pastors are too dignified and self-righteous to confront a pastor's wife or bring her to order, and many want to maintain good relations with everybody, so they will not rebuke and correct wives who are out of order [7]. But if a Jezebel is allowed to go uncorrected, you may lose everything, just as Elijah lost his ministry [7]. One man of God confessed that the greatest mistake of his life was that they did not confront the woman; they should have stepped in and stopped the Jezebel in her tracks, and because they failed, it cost them everything [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 4 and 21 of *Jezebel, A Woman Out Of Order* and chapter 15 of *Can’t You Do
Just a Little Bit More?*.

Scriptures referenced: Revelation 2:20.

items.question: What should someone who just gave their life to Christ learn first?
items.text:
What a joy to hear of a new life in Christ. The books say that anyone who comes to Christ will have to be taught the elementary principles of the faith, and that the way you are taught these fundamentals permanently determines your spiritual make-up [2]. They also point to the one who led you to Christ as the most special person in your life, someone never to be forgotten, since your greatest treasure is your salvation [2].

Beyond that, the books encourage a new believer to be active in ministry right away — soul winning, following up converts, singing and playing for the Lord — and to keep that alongside your other pursuits, as the author did from the day he gave his life to Christ [3][4][6]. They also urge you to remember your Creator in the days of your youth, as Ecclesiastes 12:1 says, because you may never grow old enough to repent later [8].

items.question: How should a Christian live simply and avoid wasting money?
items.text:
Our books speak to this plainly. Wasting what God has put in your hand costs you your position and your prosperity: the steward was told to give an account, "for thou mayest be no longer steward" (Luke 16:1-2), and the prodigal "wasted his substance with riotous living" until he began to be in want (Luke 15:12-14) [1]. When you can stop the things that waste away your money, you will become rich [1]. So cut out waste, and do not have an expensive lifestyle — cut your coat according to your size, and avoid grandiose and expensive things that others may be doing [6]. Develop a dislike for loans and gifts, for every admirer of gifts and loans is likely to fail in leadership, and many people do not pay back their loans [6].

Watch your company too, for the prodigal did not waste his money alone — there were harlots to help him do so (Luke 15:25), and evil company corrupts good habits (1 Corinthians 15:33) [3]. Bad company will cause you to waste your life away [3]. And beware of lust for things apart from God's Word, for the lusts of other things entering in choke the word and it becomes unfruitful (Mark 4:19); such desires destroy [5]. There are no short cuts — be wary of get-rich-quick schemes, for the Kingdom of Heaven is like a mustard seed that needs time to grow [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 14 of *He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath*, chapter 10 of *Opportunities*, chapters 3 and 4 of *How you can become a strong Christian* and chapter 2 of *What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 30:3-6; Psalms 27:4; Mark 4:19; Luke 15:12-14; Luke 15:25; Luke 16:1-2; 1 Corinthians 15:33.

items.question: Different topic: how do I pray effectively?
items.text:
On praying effectively, our books say to learn to pray all day and all night long, and that you will experience one hundred per cent answers to your prayers [8]. There are times you need to spend many hours in prayer, and if Jesus had to pray for long hours, then you will also have to; you can pray on the same topic for hours, and that is not useless repetition, it is praying like Jesus did [8].

They also speak of praying with strong crying and tears, as Hebrews 5:7 says Jesus offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears [8]. And they call us to the prayer of thanksgiving: "In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you" (1 Thessalonians 5:18), and as you thank Him you will experience many breakthroughs [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *How to Pray*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Thessalonians 5:18; Hebrews 5:7.

items.question: How can I pray more effectively?
items.text:
Prayer that works is not doodling and dawdling — it is effectual, fervent prayer, and James 5:16 tells us that the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man avails much [1]. So let your prayers be guided by the Word of God, praying the very prayers recorded in Scripture, such as Ephesians 1:17-19 and Ephesians 3:15-19, and become a Word person, believing the Word more than you believe in yourself [1]. Pray fervently — ardently, with passion and feeling, so that anyone watching could describe your prayer as burning and eager [3]. Pray in tongues, as Paul boasted, "I thank God that I speak in tongues more than you all" (1 Corinthians 14:18) [3]. And let prayer be a two-way affair: speak to the Holy Spirit and hear His voice, for the Comforter whom the Father sends teaches you all things (John 14:26) [3].

Make it habitual, for prayer must be habitual to be effective, and pray without ceasing (1 Thessalonians 5:17) — on the bus, in the office, in the shower [4]. Enter your closet, for there is a difference between praying alone and praying with a group, and expanding your ability to pray alone expands your ability to achieve great things in prayer [6]. Develop the ability and the formula for praying four times a day — morning, afternoon, evening and all-the-time — meeting God in the morning before you meet the devil and the circumstances of life [6]. And watch and pray: watching involves staying up at night to pray, and if you learn to stay awake at night and pray, you will pray many more hours than those who merely fast and pray [8].

items.question: I keep saying hurtful things when I am angry. How do I control my mouth?
items.text:
The books speak to this. Death and life are in the power of the tongue, and no man can tame his tongue on his own — it takes the Holy Spirit to help the believer control it [3][7]. So the first thing is to bring your tongue to God rather than trusting your own strength.

Practically, the passages warn that anger and wrath are signs of lingering unforgiveness, and we are told to put away bitterness, wrath, anger, clamour and evil speaking, being kind and tenderhearted, forgiving one another as God for Christ's sake has forgiven us (Ephesians 4:31-32) [5]. Love is not easily provoked, and we are told not to let the sun go down on our wrath (Ephesians 4:26) [1]. Also, give no place to the devil (Ephesians 4:27) and give no opportunity to your flesh [6].

One caution: the passages do not describe a step-by-step method for controlling your mouth in the moment of anger, so I would not want to invent one for you.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 60 of *Model Marriage*, chapter 1 of *Poison: Taming The Tongue*, chapter 4 of *Forgiveness Made Easy 3rd Edition* and chapter 2 of *Seven Great Principles*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 18:21; 2 Corinthians 10:5; Galatians 5:13; Ephesians 4:26-27; Ephesians 4:29; Ephesians 4:31-32; James 3:8.

items.question: How can I spend time with God every morning without getting bored?
items.book: How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day
items.text:
What a good question, pastor. The books speak directly to this. The morning time with God is meant to be a relationship, not a duty — "During quiet time you develop the most important relationship of your life," and a natural relationship develops between any two people who spend quality time together [2]. Boredom often creeps in when we forget we are meeting a Person.

Practically, the books point to feeding your spirit on the Word: a daily Quiet Time of Bible study and prayer is the most consistent way to feed your spirit, and your spirit does not grow unless it is fed on the Word of God [1]. They also suggest variety within that time — listening to preaching and church services, since "faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God" (Romans 10:17) [1], and praying in tongues, which builds you up in the faith [1]. A daily dose of the Word will increase your faith [7], and a daily quiet time drives away weariness, dejection and depression, like rain and snow that cools and refreshes (Isaiah 55:10) [7]. The books also commend praying at dawn, rising "a great while before day" as Jesus did (Mark 1:35), which helps you develop one of the most important habits of your life and grow in the Word [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *How to be Born again & Avoid Hell*, chapters 3 and 6 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day* and chapter 13 of *Everything By Prayer 

Nothing Without Prayer*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 3:1-3; Isaiah 55:10; Mark 1:34-36; Romans 1:16; Romans 10:17; James 4:8; 1 Peter 2:2.

items.question: And how should I deal with them once I notice it?
items.text:
Friend, the books say disloyalty doesn't happen overnight — becoming disloyal is a process, and most people are unaware of it, so you must learn to detect it [2]. The Lord showed the author eight stages a person goes through, beginning with an independent spirit, where the rules of the organization no longer control him and he does what he wants in spite of contrary instructions [2]. That stage is so subtle that most people do not recognize it for what it actually is [2]. You can also watch the outward symptoms, since loyalty and disloyalty are things of the heart and cannot easily be seen [6]: disobedience is an outward manifestation of a disloyal heart, and disobedient people often have a rebellious streak [6]; inflexibility is another, for the stubborn person will not adapt or take correction, as Saul argued with Samuel instead of accepting the evidence of his disobedience [3]; and a disloyal assistant is quick to say, "I knew all along that this would not work," because he never fully supported the idea [8].

As for dealing with them, the books give more than one method. One is expulsion: the biblical treatment for scornful people is expulsion, and failure to dismiss someone who must go is weak leadership — like allowing a snake to live under your children's bed [5]. The author says he has used this method, and though painful, a new spirit of loyalty entered the church [5]. Another is the marking and avoiding method, from Romans 16:17-18, which teaches that people who cause divisions must be noted and avoided at all costs — to mark means to brand or label so the person can be recognized from afar [5]. The author applied this by informing some people that a brother was a doubtful person who should be avoided, without even giving the details of his misdemeanours [5]. The books also say a disloyal person is unfit for the work of God and worthless for good work of any kind, so you rather have to protect yourself from disloyal people [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills discusses this in chapters 2 and 8 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty* and chapters 7 and 12 of *Those Who Are Ignorant*.

Scriptures referenced: Romans 16:17-18; 1 Samuel 15:22-23.

items.question: How do I become a better leader of people?
items.text:
What a good thing to want, pastor. The books say plainly that if you are called to the ministry, you are called to leadership, and that good things do not drop on you like ripe mangoes from a tree — you have to study and discover what there is to learn, deciding to be a good minister of Jesus Christ [4].

At the heart of it, to lead is to work on people until they become better human beings, as Jesus did with his disciples over three years, so that others took knowledge of them that they had been with Jesus (Acts 4:13) [1]. That means reproducing yourself in others rather than making a whole lot of people dependent on one person, preparing them for the day you are no longer around, as Jesus did when he said, "A little while, and ye shall not see me" (John 16:16) [3]. And it takes wisdom, for by wisdom kings reign (Proverbs 8:15-16) — wisdom is the master key to the leadership skills you need for ministry [5].

Practically, the books urge you to value people, since people are attracted to places where they are valued and every person who feels undervalued will move away [7]; to be at peace with those around you and to bring peace between people, following peace with all men (Hebrews 12:14) [2]; to listen to people's problems, let conversation centre on others rather than yourself, encourage, say thank you, smile, and not be partial, for the wisdom from above is without partiality (James 3:17) [6]; and to get people to follow you somewhere by being yourself, believing totally in where you are going, and going there yourself first [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2, 20, 23, 79, 86, 121 and 126 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition* and chapter 4 of *Wisdom Is the Principle Thing For Your Minsitry*.

Scriptures referenced: Ruth 4:15; 1 Samuel 1:8; 2 Samuel 18:3; Proverbs 8:15-16; Proverbs 8:20; Matthew 10:17; Matthew 20:16; Mark 1:17; John 16:4-5; John 16:16 and 7 more.

items.question: How can they come back?
items.text:
The books name several causes. Shallow roots are a big one: some receive the Word with joy but have no root, and in the time of testing they fall away, as Luke 8:13 says [2]. Along with that, disappointment in a Christian leader can destabilize believers, since leaders are human and can disappoint you beyond measure [1]. Sinfulness plays a part too, for many who walk out of church had been living in sin, and they grow annoyed when their pastors preach about it [3]. Bitterness and unresolved hurts isolate a person and make them vulnerable, as Hebrews 12:15 warns [3]. Fornication also brings evil spirits into a life, and some of those spirits can cause a person to backslide [7]. And backsliding is gradual, like walking a road with no signboards, until you slide somewhere you never expected [4].

As for coming back, the books speak of God reasoning with His people: "Come now, and let us reason together" (Isaiah 1:18), for God is a rational Being who wants to reason with you [5]. Jeremiah repeatedly urged the people, "Turn away from your wicked ways. Stop doing evil! Repent and come back to God" [4]. The books also warn that there is a point of no return, a line we must not cross [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 3, 5 and 8 of *Backsliding* and chapter 3 of *Spiritual Dangers*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 1:10; Ecclesiastes 1:9-10; Isaiah 1:18; Luke 8:13; Hebrews 12:15; Revelation 18:2-3.

items.question: How do I deal with disloyal people?
items.text:
Friend, the books speak to this plainly. The first and most important method is teaching: keep teaching the Word of God regularly, because teaching is a preventive work that fights deception, and it is only deceived people who go the way of Absalom or Lucifer [3]. Beyond that, the books say you must be fierce and resolute, not dealing with the enemy in a spirit of benevolence, because disloyalty can end a church or ministry [4].

Practically, the books counsel you to wipe out the associates of disloyal people, letting them go openly to the camp they love [1], and to cast out the scorner, since Proverbs 22:10 says "Cast out the scorner, and contention shall go out" [5]. They also say to bind a "Judas" — to restrict him rather than let him operate freely [7] — and that disloyal, disobedient workers should be dismissed completely, even longstanding ones, while still making financial provision so they can live and work elsewhere, so that the root of bitterness does not spread, as Hebrews 12:15 warns [8]. The books add that absolute evidence is not needed to deal with mysterious characters; being mysterious is deemed enough for dismissal [8].

One caution the books give: do not try to be wiser than God in handling such people, but handle them God's way [7].

items.question: A teenager in our youth group says he cuts himself when he is sad.
items.text:
That is a heavy thing to carry, and I'm glad you're walking with him in it. Our books speak directly to this: the madman of Gadara, fully under the influence of Satan, cut himself with stones, and this is described as a very important manifestation of the presence of Satan — self-destruction [8]. Self-destruction is one of the key strategies of demonic attacks; when the spirit of Satan takes hold of a person, he will often begin to cut himself with stones [2].

The books also say that what makes people so sad that they give up on life can only be demons, and that perhaps evil spirits are making a person depressed and sorrowful — with the encouragement to receive deliverance in the name of Jesus [3]. They note too that suicide is a common symptom of depression and can occur in other mental conditions such as schizophrenia and bipolar disorder [5], and that people with depression are suicidal [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 9 and 11 of *Demons and How to Deal with Them* and chapters 14 and 22 of *Those who are mad*.

items.question: How do I deal with demonic attacks on my family?
items.book: Demons and How to Deal with Them
items.text:
Our books speak to this. Attacks that involve stealing, killing and destruction are caused by the devil and his agents, and spending time to bind demonic powers and destroy their plans will protect you from such evil attacks [1]. When you deal with thieves, murderers and destroyers you are dealing with Satan himself, so deal with the devil in your life by dealing properly with them [1].

It also helps to identify what you are facing, for demons and demonic activity must be identified in order to deal with them; ask God to reveal the real identity of the spirits harassing you [4]. Persistent, unusual evils are a sign of demonic activity, as Job experienced persistent attacks on his family, his life and his health [5]. And you can tighten your security: staying with the truth and avoiding deception, practicing righteousness and avoiding sin, and emphasizing salvation all tighten the security of your spirit man against demons [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 18 of *One of You is a Devil*, chapter 20 of *Demons and How to Deal with Them* and chapters 5 and 24 of *Know Your Invisible Enemies*.

Scriptures referenced: Job 1:12; Mark 5:3; Mark 5:5; Luke 8:30; John 10:10; Ephesians 6:14.

items.question: How can I tell when someone in my team is becoming disloyal?
items.text:
Friend, the books say disloyalty doesn't happen overnight — it's a process, and most people don't even notice it in themselves or in those they work with [1]. The first stage is an independent spirit: the person is still part of the church but does what he wants despite contrary instructions, obeying only the instructions he thinks are important [1].

Watch too for the signs: those who absent themselves when the church is going through hard times, since it's in times of pressure that you see a person's true character [2]; inflexibility, where someone is stubborn, unwilling to go beyond what is stipulated, and won't take correction [3]; and assistants who are glad when things go wrong, or who have no comment to make on your suggestions and vision [5]. The books also warn that where there is criticism, murmuring, and fault-finding against leaders, there is demonic activity at work [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2, 5 and 8 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*, chapter 7 of *Those Who Are Ignorant* and chapter 5 of *Know Your Invisible Enemies*.

Scriptures referenced: John 6:70; John 7:5.

items.question: What should I read during it?
items.book: How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day
items.text:
You're asking the right question, and our books give a clear path. Begin with prayer — praise and thank the Lord for another day, thank Him for who He is and what He has done, and ask Him to speak to you [5]. Then read a passage from the Bible expecting God to speak to you, praying as Psalm 119:18 says, "Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law" [5]. As for what to read, you can choose a book of the Bible and read a few verses every day, always remembering where you ended so you can continue from the same place the next day — the author had wonderful quiet times reading through Luke and Ephesians in the New Testament, and Genesis and 1st and 2nd Samuel in the Old [5]. Or you can choose a personality from the Bible whose life story you follow, since a few verses about Moses will give you much revelation for your life [5].

As you read, move into deeper study and make further references to the things that strike you, looking through the passage for what it teaches about the nature of God, a promise to believe, a command to obey, a warning to heed, or a prayer to pray [4][8]. A good reference Bible helps here, and you may also use a daily Bible reading guide, which is very helpful in developing a regular quiet time habit [4][8]. Then write down whatever the Lord tells you, and finish by spending time praying to the Lord and listening to the voice of the Holy Spirit [4][8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills covers this in chapter 8 of *Key Facts for New Believers* and chapters 3 and 11 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalm 119:18; Exodus 34:2-3; Ephesians 1:17.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3 and 11 of *The Secret* and chapter 8 of *Key Facts for New Believers*.

items.question: What does it mean to be a shepherd over a small group of people?
items.book: What It Means to Become a Shepherd
items.text:
Being a shepherd over a small group means you are a caring, loving guide to the sheep God has entrusted to you [3]. You see them as sheep and relate with them as such, giving your time to care, to love, to feed and to gather them [1]. It is a work of loving, caring and guiding, so much so that the sheep end up calling their shepherds fathers [6].

It is also a privilege: you help people to prosper, you provide good food for them, and you lead them [5]. You lead them beside still waters and to green pastures, guide them through wilderness situations, and lead them like a flock [7]. And it is an honour to be chosen from among men, to have a job in things pertaining to God, to relate to God directly on behalf of people, and to be chosen to have compassion on the ignorant [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*, chapters 2 and 3 of *The Privilege* and chapter 20 of *The Art of Shepherding*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 23:1-2; Psalms 77:20; Psalms 78:52-54; Psalms 95:6-7; Matthew 9:36; John 21:16.
